title: The deterministic seam in the harness
summary: **The seam.** Everything on the verifiable side of the dashed line is a pure function of its input: a dict lookup, a FIFO queue, and a registry of handlers. Only inside `run()` does non-determinism enter — and even there, an agent with no API key falls back to keyword and regex extraction rather than failing. The `requires_human_review` flag on the result is the single most consequential field in the codebase: it decides whether an artifact lands on `main` or lands in a pull request.

title: What BaseAgent hands every agent
summary: An agent author writes `run()`. Timing, retries, metering, the audit trail, shared memory and events come from the base class.

cards.label: `run(trigger)`
cards.detail: The only thing an agent author writes. Abstract; enforced by `ABC`.

cards.label: `execute(trigger)`
cards.detail: Wraps `run()` with timing, a run ID, token accounting and exception capture. A crash becomes a failed `AgentResult`, never a stack trace out of the queue.

cards.label: `call_claude(...)`
cards.detail: The single LLM door. Auto-detects Gemini or Anthropic from the environment. `temperature=0.0`, 3 retries, backoff doubling from 1s on rate limits and 5xx.

cards.label: `load_prompt(file, **kw)`
cards.detail: Reads from `prompts/*.txt` and substitutes with `string.Template`. Never an inline prompt string.

cards.label: `.wiki`
cards.detail: Lazy handle on SharedMemory — the namespaced project wiki every agent reads and writes.

cards.label: `.events` / `emit()`
cards.detail: Publishes a typed event to the EventBus. The agent does not know or care who subscribes.

cards.label: `StructuredLogger`
cards.detail: Writes every run as a JSON line to `pipeline/logs/agent_runs.jsonl` — the audit trail.

cards.label: `MetricsCollector`
cards.detail: Records per-call tokens, latency, model, prompt file and estimated cost; per-run duration, success and review flag. Wrapped so metrics can never break execution.

title: Three checkpoints, at three layers
summary: A flag on the result, a gate between runs, and a hard stop before any plan exists.

cards.label: The flag
cards.detail: `requires_human_review` plus a structured `review_items` list on the agent’s result. Set at ten call sites across six agents. It propagates to the step record, the pipeline record and the wiki entry, which is tagged `human_review`.

cards.label: The pull request
cards.detail: CI-run pipelines cannot write to `main` — they can only open a PR labelled `agent-generated`, `needs-human-review`. Artifacts are drafts until a person merges, and downstream agents read the merged state on the next run.

cards.label: The refusal
cards.detail: The planning agent will not emit a plan at all while any blocking question is unanswered, and stamps every plan it does emit `awaiting review — no code may start until accepted`. A hard stop rather than a flag.

title: Five layers, cheapest first
summary: L1 and L2 cost nothing to run, so they block every pull request. L3 and L4 spend human time. Only L5 spends tokens, and only on demand.

title: 95 commits, 17 April to 2 September
summary: Dates from the repository’s git log. The turning point is the 24 July coaching session; the quality layer landed five days later.

events.label: First commit, then infrastructure
events.detail: Two commits before any agent exists. The scaffolding comes first.

events.label: The framework lands in one move
events.detail: `SES framework: agents, pipelines, orchestrator, dashboards, docs`. Then, the same day, the corrections start: Jira MCP rewritten for the new `/search/jql` API, a GitHub MCP client added, and a commit whose message is the honest state of things — `wire all agents to real data, fix broken PM agents`.

events.label: Traceability becomes a first-class store
events.detail: A unified store chaining concern → decision → requirement → Jira → risk, then rebuilt to 184 artifacts and 760 links with zero orphans. This is the spine that later lets a dashboard answer “which meeting caused this requirement” with provenance rather than assertion.

events.label: The agents start committing — badly, then well
events.detail: The first four `[agent:req_extractor]` commits have summaries like `REQ-001: Yeah, starting. So… I think… So the…` — raw transcript filler promoted straight to a requirement title. All four were deleted within two hours. The second pass produces the real set — `REQ-001 Automated product attribute extraction`, `REQ-002 ML confidence scoring`, `REQ-011 Exclude pricing from ML pipeline` — with the last three following on 29 April: twelve in total, each typed as `FUNCTIONAL` / `NON_FUNCTIONAL` / `CONSTRAINT` / `USER_GOAL` / `SOFT_GOAL`.

events.label: From laptop script to repository service
events.detail: Five merged pull requests in one day, and the character of the project changes. The drop-folder CI trigger, the program-health dashboard with provenance-stamped answers, weekly auto-refresh, the LLM requirements-extraction workflow, and the defect management spec plus the `/defect-triage` skill. Also a summer batch run: ten client meetings from 14 May to 16 July pushed through the pipeline at once.

events.label: The coaching session
events.detail: Cory Gwin, GitHub Copilot. Three recommendations: lean hard into deterministic QA because it consumes no tokens; define eval scenarios per skill, for regression detection; build throwaway QA interfaces for humans, not more agents. All three are now cited by name in the source files that implement them.

events.label: The quality layer lands
events.detail: `Add agent eval harness, custom SES linter, and CI quality gates` — five days after the session. Same day: the refactor, test-review and planning agents, all three registered; the QA interface for the VTT parser; and the risk register regenerated from the database rather than maintained by hand.

events.label: A requirements shift, absorbed in public
events.detail: The client moves to ETIM — a standardised electrical-products classification — and the architecture has to answer for it. Spec v1.2 through v1.4, ADRs 0016 through 0021, and a rebuilt v6 diagram. One commit is a correction of the team’s own understanding: `Correct where ETIM matching happens: ML owns it, behind attribute matching`. Another is a small masterclass in intellectual honesty: `Explain the wrong-class failure instead of asserting it`. A third, `Adopt Arjun's v4 script; drop the "same staging" contradiction`, is a teammate’s edit winning over the generated draft.

events.label: The privacy scrub
events.detail: Two commits remove every real meeting transcript, client minute and coach session, and replace real participant identities with roles and placeholders. They contained other people’s verbatim speech and client material. The pipelines now run against synthetic fixtures in `examples/`, and `pipeline/vtt_processor.py` reads real speaker identities from an uncommitted file when one is supplied. The third, and the final commit of the project, rewrites the README: `Lead with what the system verifies, not what it contains.`
